title: Is activity-based working impacting health, work performance and perceptions? A systematic review
authors: Lina Engelen, Josephine Chau, Sarah Young, Martin Mackey, Dheepa Jeyapalan & Adrian Bauman (2018)
review_question: To establish whether there is an evidence base for the effects of ABW on health, work performance, and perceptions of the physical and psychosocial work environment, and to evaluate the relative advantages and disadvantages of ABW.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included: (1) ABW concept with no allocated desk and variety of tailored work environments; (2) conducted in an office environment with adults; (3) measured health, work performance, or perceptions of the physical/psychosocial work environment; (4) pre-post, natural experiment, post-occupancy, or case study designs; (5) full-text articles available in English. Excluded: Active design, mobile working, IT systems, agile projects, hot desking only, non-peer-reviewed publications.

synthesis_conclusions: Activity-based working (ABW) has positive outcomes in the areas of interaction, communication, control of time and space, and satisfaction with the workspace.
There is limited evidence for the effects of ABW on physical and mental health.

ABW is a promising concept that can provide benefits for work performance and perceptions of the work environment when coupled with flexible design based on needs assessment, appropriate management support, and organization.
evidence_gaps: Lack of objective measures and evidence on health and health behavioural effects of ABW.
Need for consistent and appropriate evidence-generating research methods and designs across disciplines to ensure comparability.
Health outcomes need to be more specific than 'overall health' to tease out physical, mental, or organizational effects.
Impacts of ABW on health and wellbeing must be examined using a cross-disciplinary collaborative approach.
More research is needed to determine the implications of ABW introduction in the public sector.
risk_of_bias_assessment: A basic assessment of the quality of the included studies was made based on study design, sample size, number of workplaces, statistical analyses, description of sample characteristics, and response rates (Table 2). Quality scores varied from 4 to 11 out of 13.
heterogeneity_sources: Diversity of disciplines conducting and reporting on ABW settings and their effects.
Variation in research methods due to multidisciplinary backgrounds of researchers.
Differences in study design (qualitative, pre-post, post-occupancy, case study).
Differences in sample size (12 to 11,799 participants).
Differences in scientific rigour in reporting and analyses.
Lack of clear descriptions of the former situation before ABW adoption.
Limited generalizability to other cultures due to literature being mostly from the Netherlands.
Most studies based in corporate industry with limited information about the public sector.
limitations: The included studies were from a range of disciplines, and of varying quality, with differences in study design, sample size, and scientific rigour in reporting and analyses, limiting strong conclusions.
Variation in research methods due to multidisciplinary backgrounds of researchers investigating ABW.
Post-only studies provide weaker evidence of causality compared to more rigorous methods.
Lack of clear descriptions of the former situation before ABW adoption, limiting quantification of change.
Limited generalizability to other cultures due to most literature being from the Netherlands.
Most studies are based in the corporate industry, with limited information about the public sector where less positive outcomes are reported.

environmental_features: variety of work settings (e.g., quiet rooms, focus booths, collaboration zones, meeting rooms)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: continuous 8-hour workday over periods ranging from several months to multiple years

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The impact of activity-based working depends on the congruence between the environment's characteristics and individuals' needs, preferences, and tasks.

Activity-based working environments introduce new job demands (e.g., noise, lack of privacy) and job resources (e.g., autonomy, variety of settings) that influence employee well-being and performance.
The effectiveness of activity-based working is influenced by the interplay between the physical environment (technical system) and the social organization and work processes (social system).
Individuals' responses to stressors in activity-based working environments (e.g., noise, lack of privacy) are mediated by their coping strategies and perceived control.

mechanism_chain.description: Activity-based working environments can impact health, work performance, and perceptions through various pathways related to environmental characteristics, individual experiences, and psychological states.
